definition: A test that adjusts to you as you go. On the GMAT Focus each answer changes the difficulty of later questions in that section.
example: Answer a hard question right and the next one tends to be harder.

definition: The GMAT adapts after every single question, not after blocks of questions.
The share of test takers you scored higher than. A 90th percentile means you beat about 90 percent of them.
example: A total score and its percentile appear on your score report.

definition: The overall GMAT Focus score on a 205 to 805 scale in steps of 10, ending in 5 (for example 655).
The score for Quant, Verbal or Data Insights, each from 60 to 90.
A GMAC feature that builds your best possible total from the strongest section scores across valid Focus Edition attempts.
A feature that lets you bookmark questions in a section and change up to three answers before you finish it.
A flag you place on a question so you can find it again in Review & Edit.
A scoring penalty applied when you leave questions blank at the end of time. Always answer everything, even with a guess.

A paid report that GMAC has offered in the past, breaking your performance down by question type and timing. GMAC now says detailed insights are free on the Official Score Report, so confirm on mba.com whether the paid version still exists before buying.
The score report schools receive. You see the official version after the exam; free sends go to five programs.
The preview score shown on screen right after you finish the exam, before the official report arrives.
The ability to take Quant, Verbal and Data Insights in any order you choose at the start of the exam.
A single 10-minute break you can take between sections.
Taking the GMAT again. You can test up to 5 times in 12 months, with 16 days between attempts.
A Pearson VUE site where you can take the GMAT in person. Original passport is required in India.
The at-home version of the GMAT, taken with a proctor watching remotely.
The writing surface supplied for your rough work, because your own paper and pens are not allowed in the exam.
How long a score can be sent to schools. GMAT scores are valid for five years.
The Graduate Management Admission Council, the organisation that owns and runs the GMAT.
A standard five-choice math question. All 21 Quant questions on the GMAT Focus are Problem Solving.
A whole number, positive, negative or zero. 3, 0 and −7 are integers; ½ is not.
A whole number greater than 1 whose only factors are 1 and itself. 2 is the only even prime.
A whole number greater than 1 that is not prime; it has more than two factors.
A number that divides another evenly. 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12 are all factors of 12.
A number you get by multiplying a given number by an integer. Multiples of 5 are 5, 10, 15 and so on.
Dividing evenly with remainder zero. 12 is divisible by 4 because 12 ÷ 4 = 3 exactly.
What is left over after division. 17 ÷ 5 gives quotient 3 and remainder 2, since 17 = 5 × 3 + 2.
The whole-number result of a division, ignoring the remainder.
The largest number that divides two or more numbers evenly. GCF of 12 and 18 is 6.
The smallest positive number that is a multiple of each number. LCM of 4 and 6 is 12.
Writing a number as a product of primes. 60 = 2² × 3 × 5.
Even numbers are divisible by 2; odd numbers are not. Even + even is even, odd × odd is odd.
Integers in order with no gaps, like 7, 8, 9. Their difference is always 1.
The distance of a number from zero, always non-negative. |−5| = 5.
The number you multiply by to get 1. The reciprocal of 3/4 is 4/3.
A small raised number saying how many times to multiply the base by itself. 2⁵ = 32.
The non-negative number that multiplies by itself to give the original. √49 = 7.
The square of an integer, such as 1, 4, 9, 16, 25.
The product of all positive integers up to n, written n!. 5! = 120. By definition 0! = 1.
A comparison of quantities. A ratio of 3:2 means 3 parts to 2 parts.
An equation saying two ratios are equal, like 3/4 = 9/12.
Parts per hundred. 35% means 35/100 or 0.35.
The change divided by the original, times 100. From 50 to 65 is a 30% increase.
The simple difference between two percentages. From 20% to 25% is 5 percentage points.
Interest paid only on the original amount: I = P × r × t.
Interest paid on the original amount plus past interest: A = P(1 + r)<sup>t</sup> for annual compounding.
The sum of the values divided by how many there are.
The middle value when the numbers are in order; the average of the two middle values if there is an even number.
The value that appears most often in a set.
The largest value minus the smallest value in a set.
A measure of how spread out numbers are around the mean. A small SD means values cluster near the mean.
An average where some values count more than others, based on how often they occur.
An equation where the variable has no exponent above one, like 3x + 5 = 20.
An equation with a squared variable, like x² − 5x + 6 = 0. It can have up to two roots.
A statement comparing two expressions with <, >, ≤ or ≥. Flip the sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative.
A rule that gives exactly one output for each input, written f(x).
A list where each term differs from the last by a constant, like 4, 7, 10, 13.
A list where each term is the previous one times a constant ratio, like 3, 6, 12, 24.
An arrangement where order matters. Choosing a president then a secretary from 5 people: 5 × 4 = 20.
A selection where order does not matter. Choosing a team of 2 from 5 people: 5C2 = 10.
How likely an event is: favourable outcomes divided by total equally likely outcomes. Always between 0 and 1.
Events where one outcome does not change the probability of the other. Multiply their probabilities for 'and'.
Events that cannot both happen. Their 'or' probability is the plain sum.
A problem where some items belong to more than one group. Use Total = A + B − Both + Neither.
A picture of overlapping circles showing which items belong to which groups.
How much of something happens per unit of time. Speed is distance per time; work rate is job per time.
A problem where two or more solutions or items are combined, and you track the amount of the key ingredient.
The last digit of a number. Powers of integers follow repeating units-digit cycles.
A set where consecutive terms differ by the same amount. Mean and median are equal.
A conclusion supported by one or more premises. Critical Reasoning questions ask you to analyse one.
A stated fact or reason offered as evidence for a conclusion.
The main claim an argument is trying to prove. Look for words like 'therefore' or 'so'.
An unstated idea the argument needs for its conclusion to follow from its premises.
A statement that must be true for the argument to work. If you negate it, the argument breaks.
A check for assumptions: negate the answer choice, and if the argument falls apart, the choice is a necessary assumption.
A conclusion that must be true given the information. In RC it is a small logical step beyond the text.
A question type asking for a fact that makes the conclusion more likely to be true.
A question type asking for a fact that makes the conclusion less likely to be true.
A question type asking which piece of information would best help you judge the argument.
A CR question where two facts seem to conflict, and you find the fact that resolves the conflict.
A CR question asking what role two highlighted statements play in the argument, such as premise or conclusion.
An error in the reasoning, for example confusing correlation with cause.
Two things happening together does not prove one causes the other. A third cause or reverse direction may explain it.
A point raised against a claim, often introduced by 'however' or 'critics argue'.
A different explanation for an effect, used to weaken a causal argument.
When the group studied does not represent the larger population, making the conclusion unreliable.
The range of topics an argument or passage covers. Answers outside the scope are usually wrong.
Words like always, never, all, only. Answers with such words are usually too strong to be supported.
Restating an idea in different words. Correct RC answers often paraphrase the passage.
The central point of the whole passage, not just one paragraph.
What the author is trying to do in the passage: describe, argue, compare, explain, or critique.
The author's attitude, such as critical, neutral, enthusiastic or skeptical.
A brief note on scratch paper summarising what each paragraph does, to find details quickly later.
A word like 'however' or 'moreover' that signals the direction of the argument.
An RC question asking why the author included a detail, not what the detail says.
An RC question asking you to apply the passage's idea to a new situation.
An answer choice discussing something the argument or passage never mentions.
A wrong answer designed to look right, often using words from the passage.
In Data Sufficiency, information that gives a single definite answer to the question.
A question with two statements where you decide if they give enough information to answer, without necessarily solving it.
A DS question asking for a specific number. A statement is sufficient only if it fixes one value.
A DS question asking whether something is true. A statement is sufficient only if it always gives the same answer.
A Data Insights question type using a sortable table with statements to judge as true or false.
A table on screen you can reorder by any column to find rankings, extremes and medians quickly.
A question with a chart or graph and a sentence with two drop-down menus to complete.
A question with a scenario where you choose one answer for each of two linked parts.
A set of two or three tabs of information (text, tables, charts) with several questions drawing on them.
The skill of reading, interpreting and drawing sound conclusions from data.
A basic calculator available only in the Data Insights section.
One of the reference lines of a chart, labelled with a variable and units. Always read both axes.
A chart showing individual data points to reveal a relationship or trend between two variables.
A line summarising the general direction of data on a scatter plot.
A data point far from the others. It can pull the mean but barely affects the median.
Approximating a number to simplify arithmetic. In DI, round carefully and check the answer options' spacing.
Managing your time so each question gets its fair share. Roughly 2 minutes per question on average.
Making an educated guess when stuck, so you keep time for later questions rather than burning minutes on one.
Removing answer choices you can prove wrong, which improves your odds when guessing.
Replacing variables with easy numbers to test an expression or choose an answer.
Testing the answer choices in the problem, starting with the middle one, instead of solving algebraically.
Approximating to rule out answers, especially when choices are far apart.
A notebook or file where you record every mistake, why it happened, and the fix, so you stop repeating it.
Reviewing material at increasing intervals, which fixes it in long-term memory better than cramming.
Testing yourself from memory instead of rereading. Flashcards and practice questions are active recall.
A full-length timed practice test used to measure your score and stamina under exam conditions.
An early test that shows your strengths and weaknesses so you can plan your study.
Reducing study load in the final days before the exam so you arrive rested and sharp.
Choosing the order of Quant, Verbal and Data Insights, usually to start with your strongest section or rest your weakest.
Giving a task a fixed amount of time and stopping when it runs out.
A planned sequence for exam morning: sleep, food, ID, travel, warm-up, so decisions are removed.
The belief that ability improves through effort and good practice, which suits a skill like the GMAT.

One of the fixed deadlines (Round 1, 2, 3) a school sets for applications. Earlier rounds often have more scholarship money and seats, though some schools say the round does not materially change your chances.
A process where applications are reviewed as they come in and decided on a continuing basis rather than at fixed deadlines.
An arrangement letting an admitted student start a year later, sometimes offered to those with early career plans.
The percentage of admitted students who accept the offer. Schools watch it closely.
A holding list of candidates not yet admitted or rejected. Spots open if admitted people decline.
A reference written by a manager or colleague who knows your work, a required part of most MBA applications.
A one-year or two-year masters for early-career candidates, often with little or no work experience.
Master of Business Administration, typically for candidates with several years of work experience.
The name many Indian business schools use for their full-time MBA-equivalent programme, for example the one-year PGP at ISB.
What you gain from the degree compared with what it costs. Salary uplift divided by total cost is the common view.
A non-profit that supports women in business school with fellowships, events and community.
The published statistics for a school's current cohort, including average GMAT, work experience and countries.
The typical score of admitted students, published in the class profile. A guide, not a cut-off.
A written piece explaining your goals and why this programme fits.
A conversation, often by invitation, where the school tests fit and communication.
Years of professional experience, which schools weigh alongside your score and academic record.
Funding awarded on merit or need, which reduces what you pay.
A permit letting international graduates work in the country after finishing, which affects ROI for study-abroad plans.
A US programme classification that can allow longer post-study work authorisation for international students.
An alternative graduate admissions test that many business schools also accept.
The Common Admission Test used for entry to IIMs and many Indian business schools.
How well your goals, background and values match what a programme offers.
An applicant using an MBA to move to a new function or industry.
Sending your official GMAT score to a school. Five free sends are included with the exam.
An essay for explaining weaknesses, such as a low grade or a career gap.
